newsitem.title: USA: Wheat, oats prices rise amid Canada shipping delays.
newsitem.headline: Wheat, oats prices rise amid Canada shipping delays.

text.p: Wheat prices soared Tuesday due to serious shipping delays at Canadian grain ports that could lure foreign buyers to the United States.

Oat prices also rose because Canada's shipping delays might cut the flow of imported oats into the United States. Coffee prices rose again due to a nationwide strike in Colombia that might hurt exports.

About 1.5 million metric tons of Canadian wheat exports have been delayed since January due to severe winter weather, and the delays may back up February and March shipments as well. The weather slowed railroads from delivering Canadian wheat to western ports.

There were market rumours Tuesday that some Asian buyers, concerned about the delays, diverted ships to U.S. Pacific Northwest ports to load U.S. wheat rather than Canadian. Additionally, the Canadian Wheat Board commissioner said the delays were becoming worse.
"The situation is deteriorating. There are 13 ships due this week; if they all show up we'll be further behind," said Canadian Wheat Board chief Commissioner Lorne Hehn.
Hehn also said the delays may extend into April.

At the Chicago Board of Trade soft red winter wheat for March delivery closed up 9-1/2 cents at $3.62 per bushel, posting much of the gain late the session immediately after Hehn's comments. Kansas City Board of Trade hard red winter wheat for March also rose 9-1/2 cents to $4.23-1/2. Minneapolis Grain Exchange March spring wheat rose 5-3/4 cents to $3.88-1/4.
CBOT oat futures closed sharply higher on talk of delays in shipping Canadian oats to the United States, traders said.
"There was talk of four to six week delays in railing oats to the U.S.," a trader said.
The United States does not produce enough oats to meet demand and must import, largely from Canada.
CBOT March oats closed up 9-3/4 cents at $1.77-1/4 per bushel. The daily trading limit is 10 cents.
Coffee futures at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange rose to contract highs as a nationwide strike got underway in Colombia, the world's second-largest coffee producer.

About 800,000 Colombia state workers went on strike Tuesday. The strike's impact on the coffee sector was not clear, but Colombian exporters said the strike could hit customs operations and hold up shipments from some ports.

Procter and Gamble's Folgers Coffee Co. said Tuesday it planned to raise the list price on its standard 13-ounce can of coffee by 15 cents effective March 17, due to higher prices of green coffee on the world's futures markets.
"I suppose it (Folgers price hike) is a confirmation of the shortage they perceive," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "But a price rise can limit gains because it can limit consumption."
March coffee rose to a life-of-contract high of 166.50 cents per pound before profit-taking trimmed gains. March coffee closed at 163.55 cents, up 4.90 cents.
New York Mercantile Exchange gasoline futures ended higher Tuesday on a correction after falling 7 cents a gallon since late last week.
March gasoline settled up 0.43 cent a gallon at 63.96 cents, while March crude settled 4 cents a barrel lower at $22.42. March heating oil ended 0.10 cent higher at 61.86 cents a gallon.
